newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Central bank warning seen cooling Taiwan stocks.
newsitem.headline: Central bank warning seen cooling Taiwan stocks.

text.p: Taiwan shares were likely to go through a correction period after the central bank pleaded for caution in a rising stock market, analysts said on Sunday.
But they did not expect to see moves to tighten monetary policy immediately.
Taiwan's central bank deputy governor Hsu Chia-tung said on Saturday that individual investors should exercise caution following the recent stock market rally.

"Individual investors, especially those using margin loans in trading, should 'think about danger when reaching highs'," Hsu told reporters. He was speaking after the stock market closed 1.38 percent higher on Saturday at a six-year high.
The index ended up 108.39 points to 7,983.71, up 15.1 percent from the start of the year.

Analysts said they did not expect the central bank's current stable-to-loose monetary policy to be tightened immediately, but said the index would likely react to Hsu's comments by falling, testing support at 7,600 next week.

"The central bank is unlikely to tighten its monetary policy in the near term. This is simply a warning, which however should be enough to cool down the overheated stock market," said David Yu, vice-president at International Investment Trust Co.

But analysts said they also did not expect to see sharp falls in the index because the government still needed a comparatively bullish stock market to support the slowly recovering economy and its plan to privatise state-run enterprises.
"If the stock market plunges, it will dampen the slowly recovering economy and hit the government's privatisation programme," said Allen Huang, a National Securities manager.
The Finance Ministry said in January it planned to release some 800 million state-owned shares worth some T$100 billion (US$3.6 billion) in fiscal 1997/98 (July/June) to alleviate its budget deficit.

Analysts said the recent stock market rallies were faster and higher than expected mainly because the government had been trying to buoy the stock market following the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping on February 19.
On February 18, central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong vowed to "closely watch" the stock market, saying share prices had risen "slightly too much."
The index has climbedn another 4.5 percent since then.
But immediately after the news of Deng's death, the cabinet said it had prepared funds to support the market against a potential plunge and would launch other market-boosting steps.

The recent rallies also reflected a recovering economy after the cabinet's statistics agency in late February announced higher-than-expected fourth quarter gross domestic product growth of 6.62 percent and raised its 1997 GDP forecast to 6.28 percent from 6.20.
